newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain cuts key rate after inflation moderates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain cuts key rate after inflation moderates.

text.p: The Bank of Spain sanctioned the fourth reduction this year in its key money market rate on Friday following a sharp moderation in inflation in April.

The central bank reduced the rate to 5.25 percent from 5.50 percent, after data on Wednesday showed Spanish inflation had fallen to 1.7 percent in April -- its lowest level in nearly three decades -- from 2.2 percent in March.
The Economy Ministry welcomed the reduction, saying it was an endorsement of the one-year-old government's economic policy.

"The decision taken today by the Bank of Spain is the consequence of a progressive clean-up of macroeconomic desequilibriums, especially in the reduction of inflation and control of the public deficit," the Ministry said.
The cut had been widely expected given improving inflation rates and the stability of the peseta against the mark.

In a Reuter survey of economists conducted on Wednesday after the inflation data, all 10 polled predicted an interest rate cut. Nine had forecast a reduction of 25 basis points and one had predicted a 50-basis-point cut.
"We were going for a 25 basis point cut after very good inflation data and the peseta has been stable," said Heather Richardson, economist at UBS in London.
Inflation is expected to moderate further in May, leading many economists to expect a further reduction in the rate in one month.
"We think that if inflation stays below two percent in May and the peseta remains stable, they could cut another 25 basis points to five percent," Richardson said.
"We've seen 12 cuts in the last 17 months. I think we'll see 13 in 18 but they can't go on forever."
But while many economists agreed there would be another cut next month, they were divided on whether that would be the last in this cycle given the outlook for an inflation pick-up.
UBS sees inflation picking up to 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter. It sees inflation at an average of 2.4 percent in 1997.
As a result, the central bank may decide to quit cutting at five percent, Richardson said.

"We believe the Bank of Spain can cut another 25 basis points to five percent next month after May CPI. Then it will have another 25 basis point scope which it is likely to use in the last quarter of the year, in October of November," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at the Bank of America in Madrid.
